check: Capture page one for your exact brand name, on desktop and mobile
why: Your brand SERP is what people (and AI systems summarising the web) see when they look you up. You need a dated baseline before changing anything.
how: Search your brand name in a private window, set to your main country and language. Screenshot page one on desktop and mobile, then log each result in the 'Brand SERP log' tab.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Record which results you own or control
why: Owned pages and official profiles are results you can keep accurate. Third-party results show how others describe you, for better or worse.
how: In the Brand SERP log, mark each result as Owned site, Official profile, Third party (positive / neutral / negative) or Namesake. The Progress tab shows your owned share.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Note which SERP features appear for your brand query and which kind of panel it is
why: A knowledge panel (an entity in Google's Knowledge Graph) and a Business Profile (a local business listing) look alike but are managed in different ways. Sitelinks, AI Overviews, videos and People Also Ask also shape the page.
how: List every feature on page one: knowledge panel, Business Profile, sitelinks, AI Overview, People Also Ask, Top stories, videos, images, social posts, reviews. Entity panels usually carry a short description (often sourced from a site such as Wikipedia) and may offer 'Claim this knowledge panel'; a panel with hours, directions and reviews is usually a Business Profile.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Check the brand + modifier searches people actually run
why: Searches like '[brand] reviews', '[brand] pricing', '[brand] vs [competitor]' and '[founder name]' are where wrong or negative information tends to surface.
how: Pull branded queries from Search Console (filter queries containing the brand). Search the top five modifiers and log anything inaccurate or unowned.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Ask AI assistants who you are and compare the answer with your canonical facts
why: AI answers draw on the same records as your knowledge panel. Wrong founding dates, products or locations point to the sources you need to correct.
how: Ask 'What is [brand]?' and 'Who founded [brand]?' in Google AI Mode, Gemini, ChatGPT and Perplexity. Compare against the Fact sheet tab and note every mismatch and the source cited.

check: Look up your brand (and founder) in the Knowledge Graph Search API
why: The API shows whether Google's Knowledge Graph holds an entity for your name, its machine ID (kg:/m/... or kg:/g/...), type and description. No entity means a recognition problem comes before anything else.
how: Use the API Explorer on Google's Knowledge Graph Search API page or the MLforSEO Knowledge Graph API notebook with your own API key. Log the ID, name, @type, description and resultScore in the 'KG lookup log' tab. Google now points new projects to Cloud Enterprise Knowledge Graph and says this API isn't for production-critical use; it is fine for audits.

check: Confirm the entity returned is you, not a namesake
why: If a famous person, place or another company with the same name comes back first, you have a disambiguation problem, and AI systems may attribute your content to the wrong entity.
how: Read the description and type of the top results. Search the API with your full name plus category (for example 'Acme Software'). Record which entity wins.

check: Open your entity's ID in Google Search to see the panel tied to it
why: Searching by machine ID shows the panel Google associates with that entity, even when your brand query shows something else.
how: Search https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=/g/XXXX (use the ID from the API without the 'kg:' prefix). Screenshot the result.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Look for duplicate or fragmented entities for your brand
why: Name variants ('Acme', 'Acme Corp', 'Acme Corporation') can create several thin entities instead of one strong one.
how: Query each name variant and your founder in the API. If more than one ID describes your organisation, note them all and make naming consistent everywhere (area 5).

check: Treat resultScore as a relative signal only
why: Google documents resultScore as an indicator of how well an entity matched the request and publishes no thresholds. It moves with the query, so compare it only with itself over time.
how: Run the same query monthly and log the score in the KG lookup log. Rising scores and a stable ID are good signs; a changing ID is worth investigating.

check: Search Wikidata for an existing item before creating anything
why: Duplicate items are the most common reason brand entries get deleted. Someone may already have created one for you.
how: Search wikidata.org for your brand, legal name and founders. Record any Q-IDs in the Fact sheet. If one exists, improve it rather than starting again.

check: If an item exists, check it is accurate, neutral and referenced
why: Wikidata is openly licensed and widely reused by search and AI systems, so errors there spread. Unreferenced statements are easy to challenge.
how: Check label, description (short and neutral, no promotional language), instance of, country, official website, inception, founders, headquarters and social media IDs. Every statement should cite an external source.

check: If there is no item, check notability before creating one
why: Wikidata accepts entities that can be described using serious, publicly available references: registries, authority records, databases and independent coverage. Your own website on its own isn't enough.
how: List your external references (company registry, Crunchbase, trade press, conference programmes, industry databases). If you have two or three solid ones, you likely qualify; if not, earn coverage first (area 6).

check: Declare any conflict of interest when you or your agency edit
why: Editing your own organisation's item or article is a conflict of interest. On Wikipedia, paid editing must be disclosed under the Wikimedia Terms of Use, and you should propose changes on the article's Talk page rather than editing directly.
how: Use a personal, clearly identifiable account. Note your connection on your user page. For Wikipedia, request edits on the Talk page with independent sources.

check: Record whether a Wikipedia article exists and is accurate
why: Wikipedia is a strong source for knowledge panels, but its notability bar (significant coverage in independent, reliable sources) excludes most small and mid-size brands. Not having one is normal.
how: Search Wikipedia in your main languages. If an article exists, log factual errors and suggest corrections on its Talk page with sources. Don't write your own article.

check: Organization (or Person / ProfilePage) markup sits on your home or about page
why: Google recommends placing Organization markup on the home page or a single page describing the organisation. It helps Google understand your details and which logo to show, including in knowledge panels. For a person, ProfilePage markup with a Person as mainEntity does the same job.
how: View Source on the home and about pages. Check for name, alternateName, legalName, url, logo, description, foundingDate, founder, address, contactPoint and sameAs. Validate with the Rich Results Test and Schema Markup Validator.

check: The logo in your markup is a crawlable image of at least 112 x 112 px
why: Google's Organization guidelines set this minimum and say the logo property helps Google choose the logo for Search results and knowledge panels.
how: Open the logo URL from the markup: it should load directly (not blocked by robots.txt), be square-friendly and look right on a white background.

check: Organization and founders have stable @id values that other markup points to
why: A stable @id lets every article, product and author page reference the same entity, so signals add up instead of scattering across separate declarations.
how: Check the Organization @id never changes between pages, and that Article publisher, Person worksFor and Product brand reference it.

check: Every sameAs link resolves to an official profile showing the same name
why: schema.org defines sameAs as a page that unambiguously indicates the item's identity. A broken or mismatched link is a failed confirmation, which is worse than no link.
how: Open each sameAs URL; log status code and displayed name in the Fact sheet. Include Wikidata, LinkedIn, Crunchbase, official social profiles and relevant industry directories.

check: Your about page states the canonical facts in plain text, matching the markup
why: Structured data should describe what is visible on the page. Plain-text facts also give AI systems and journalists something to quote.
how: Compare the about page text with the JSON-LD and the Fact sheet: name, founding date, founders, headquarters, what you do in one sentence.

check: Your brand is the most prominent entity on your home and about pages
why: If navigation labels or product names outscore your brand in entity extraction, the pages meant to define you send a weak signal.
how: Run Google's Natural Language API (or the MLforSEO no-code template) on the full page and on the main content only. Your brand should lead on salience. Use <nav>, <main> and <footer> elements.

check: Create a single source of truth for your canonical facts
why: One agreed version of each fact makes every later update quick and consistent. Without it, teams rediscover the platform list each time and miss some.
how: Fill in column B of the 'Fact sheet' tab: canonical name, legal name, founding date, founders, headquarters, website URL, one-sentence description, category, employee range, logo URL.

check: Audit every profile against the fact sheet
why: Each platform holding facts about you is a verification point for Google and AI systems. Consistent points add confidence; inconsistent ones subtract it.
how: Fill the platform columns in the Fact sheet: website and schema, LinkedIn, Crunchbase, Wikidata, Business Profile, X, YouTube, industry directories, company registry. Cells that differ from column B turn red.

check: Fix contradictions first, then fill gaps
why: A missing fact is neutral. Conflicting facts (founded 2011 here, 2013 there) are a conflict systems can't resolve, so they may drop the fact or lower confidence in the whole entity.
how: Sort the Fact sheet by red cells. Correct the platforms you control, then request corrections from third parties with a link to an authoritative source.

check: Founders and leaders have consistent, linked profiles
why: People entities reinforce the organisation. Consistent names, titles and employers across author pages, speaker bios and LinkedIn give systems a second route to recognising you.
how: Check each founder's LinkedIn, author page, speaker bios and Wikidata (if any) use the same name, title and employer. Link the person's markup to the Organization @id.

check: List the independent sources that already describe you
why: Google cross-checks your claims against external sources. Five consistent mentions in respected publications do more than fifty thin directory listings.
how: Search your brand in news, trade publications, podcasts, conference programmes, registries and databases. Log each source and whether its facts match the Fact sheet.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Plan coverage that would make your key facts independently verifiable
why: Panels appear when enough independent sources agree. Most brands need more third-party coverage before anything else moves.
how: Pick realistic targets: industry publications, podcast interviews, conference talks, guest articles, partner pages, awards. Track them in the Action plan tab.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Third-party mentions place you next to your category and peers
why: Co-occurrence with category terms, partners and competitors tells systems which 'Acme' you are and what you're relevant for.
how: Check how press and partner pages describe you. Ask for your full name plus a short category descriptor in bios and boilerplates.

check: If a knowledge panel shows, claim it through an official profile
why: Verified representatives can suggest changes to their panel and choose a featured image. Not every panel is claimable yet, so check back if the option is missing.
how: Signed in to a Google Account, search for the entity, click 'Claim this knowledge panel' at the bottom of the panel, then sign in to one of the listed official sites or profiles (such as Search Console, YouTube, X or Facebook).
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel
source_label: Google Help: get verified on Google

check: Once verified, suggest corrections with evidence and add team members
why: Feedback from verified representatives is prioritised, and edits backed by links to verifying pages are more likely to be accepted.
how: Use Feedback below the panel, flag the fact, describe the correction and link to pages that confirm it. Add colleagues as Contributors or Managers at google.com/search/contributions/manage.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel
source_label: Google Help: get verified on Google

check: Local businesses: claim and verify your Business Profile separately
why: Business Profiles look like knowledge panels but cover businesses serving customers at a location or in a service area, and are managed through Google Business Profile.
how: Claim or create the profile in Google Business Profile, verify it, and make name, address, phone, hours and website match the Fact sheet.

check: If the panel mixes you up with someone else or shows the wrong profiles, contact support
why: Google's knowledge panel help lists mixed-up entities and wrong websites or profiles as cases for its support team, and runs an account recovery process if someone else already manages your panel.
how: Follow the troubleshooting steps in Google's 'Get verified on Google' help article. Keep screenshots and links to authoritative sources ready.
source_label: Google Help: get verified on Google

check: Own more of page one for brand and brand + modifier searches
why: Official profiles, a clear site structure (for sitelinks) and pages answering pricing, reviews and comparison questions keep accurate information near the top.
how: Fill gaps from the Brand SERP log: complete official profiles, add or improve pages for top branded modifiers, link profiles from the site and markup.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel

check: Monthly: check the top five platforms and rerun the brand SERP and KG lookups
why: Third parties edit your records and Google updates panels automatically as the web changes. Small, regular checks stop drift.
how: Each month: website, LinkedIn, Wikidata, Crunchbase, Business Profile against the Fact sheet; add a new row to the KG lookup log; note SERP changes in the Brand SERP log.

check: Update every platform within a week of a material change
why: New leadership, a move, an acquisition or a rebrand makes old facts wrong everywhere at once. Stale data on Wikidata and profiles propagates to other systems.
how: Update the Fact sheet first, then work through every platform column. Add the change to the Action plan with an owner and date.

check: Quarterly: repeat the full audit and the AI answer check
why: Panels usually take months of consistent signals to appear: six to eighteen months for most brands in MLforSEO's experience. Quarterly reviews show whether the work is moving the entity.
how: Duplicate this sheet (or add a dated column to the logs), rerun every check, and compare KG ID, panel presence, owned share of page one and AI answer accuracy with last quarter.
learn_label: What it takes to earn a Google knowledge panel
